title: Heat belongs in maternity care. A new UN framework asks countries to count its toll.
subtitle: WHO and partner agencies want health services to track pregnancy and child-health outcomes alongside heat exposure. The challenge is turning those signals into protection women can actually use.
author: ATHENA

paragraphs.text: Countries are being asked to track premature births, stillbirths and other maternal and child-health outcomes alongside extreme heat, under a framework launched on 21 October by the World Health Organization and three partner UN agencies.

The initiative brings a climate hazard into the routine business of maternity clinics, hospitals and public-health surveillance. For a pregnant woman, its value will depend on whether better information leads to earlier warnings, safer care and somewhere she can escape dangerous temperatures.

Developed with the World Meteorological Organization, UNICEF and UNFPA, the framework recommends monitoring outcomes including low birthweight, hypertension in pregnancy, child deaths and health-service visits. School attendance is another proposed measure of disruption. It is guidance for countries, rather than evidence that those protections are already in place.
A warning signal, not a verdict on one pregnancy

WHO’s report proposes combining existing health records with temperature and other heat-exposure measures to identify unusual patterns. A rise in premature births during unusually hot conditions could prompt closer investigation and preparation for additional patients.

The report explicitly cautions that such patterns do not establish causation. Other influences must be examined. Its example charts use fictitious data to demonstrate the method; they are not records of a newly discovered outbreak of pregnancy complications.

There is, however, a substantial research base behind the concern. A systematic review published in Nature Medicine in November 2024 assembled 198 studies across 66 countries examining maternal, fetal and newborn health. Most studies came from high-income countries, limiting how evenly the evidence represents women’s circumstances worldwide.

In a pooled analysis of ten studies, heatwave exposure was associated with 26 per cent higher odds of preterm birth, with a 95 per cent confidence interval ranging from 8 to 47 per cent higher. That does not mean 26 per cent of exposed pregnancies ended prematurely, or that every woman’s risk increased by 26 percentage points.

The studies used different exposure measures and designs, and their results varied. The estimate describes an association across populations; it cannot determine why an individual baby was born early. Women should not be made to interpret a population statistic as a prediction about their own pregnancy.

The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention explains that heat adds strain to a cardiovascular system already adapting to pregnancy. Its clinical guidance, dated September 2025, recommends making a heat plan with patients: discussing access to cooling and water, reviewing medicines and identifying symptoms that require medical attention.

The guidance also asks clinicians to consider housing, the indoor environment and access to support. That makes the conversation more useful than simply telling someone to stay cool. A woman needs to be able to explain whether her home cools overnight, whether her work permits breaks and whether reaching a cooler place is realistic.

Those questions expose the practical limits of individual advice. If taking a break means losing income, or travelling to a cooled building means paying a fare she cannot afford, a warning alone has not removed the exposure. Health planning should account for the conditions in which its advice must be followed.

For employers, the practical questions include access to drinking water, toilets, rest and a cooler working environment. For local authorities, they include whether cooling spaces are reachable and open when needed. For maternity services, they include whether a patient can travel to care without a long wait in the heat.

WHO says the information should help authorities anticipate demand, strengthen warnings and identify communities at greatest risk. But a reporting framework does not itself supply a clinic with reliable electricity, pay for cooling or give a worker a protected break. Those decisions require budgets and accountable institutions.

For pregnant readers, the immediate implication is to raise heat exposure during antenatal appointments, including difficulties staying cool at home or work. CDC advises discussing medication risks with a clinician and not abruptly stopping prescribed medicines. A heat plan should fit the person’s health and circumstances.

The test for governments is whether surveillance changes what happens before and during the next period of extreme heat. Counting additional complications after they occur is necessary. Making it possible for women and children to avoid preventable harm is the purpose.
